newsitem.title: GREECE: Motor Oil gets maximum fine for refinery spill.
newsitem.headline: Motor Oil gets maximum fine for refinery spill.

text.p: Greece on Wednesday slapped the Motor Oil company with a 150 million drachma ($650,000) fine for extensive oil pollution at its refinery near the Corinth canal, the Merchant Marine Ministry said.

The fine, which is the maximum administrative penalty provided by Greek law, came only days after Greenpeace blockaded the refinery to protest against what it alleged was Motor Oil's lax environmental safety record.

A ministry investigating committee said a ship unloading oil at the refinery's docking facilities in August was not properly moored and blamed the ship's captain, the shipping company and the refinery for the "large and serious" oil spill.

"The ship...knowingly and with serious negligence did not moor as safely as it should and could," the report said. "The amount of oil spilled from both the ship and the loading pipe is estimated at 300 tonnes."
The accident took place as the 123,000 dwt Kriti Sea, owned by Motor Oil, was unloading crude oil during a thunderstorm in the middle of the night.
A lightning bolt struck dead a worker and the ship was detached from its moorings, breaking its loading pipe.
Greenpeace says loading at night or with bad weather is sure to cause accidents and wants Motor Oil, jointly owned by Saudi Aramco and the Vardinoyannis group, to clean up its act.
Activists from the international environmental group chained themselves to mooring buoys and loading cranes, blocking the refinery for 24 hours before coast guard commandos removed them last week.
Greek political opposition parties slammed the government for sending commandos after the activists while turning a blind eye to widespread pollution by powerful firms.
"In this case, judicial and coast guard authorities operated as servants to the big capital," the Communist party said in a statement, bringing the issue for discussion in parliament.
Motor Oil says its safety measures are above those required by Greek law and blames the spill on sudden bad weather.
The company had already paid an initial 70 million drachma ($320,000) deposit to the ministry for causing extensive oil pollution before its ship was allowed to leave port.

It could face more penalties if a criminal investigation also finds fault in its operations and brings charges against the company. A local prosecutor investigating the case has yet to report his findings.
Local residents could also seek damages after that report is released.
